title: Why Does Alcohol Make You Hungry? The Science of Drunk Munchies
excerpt: Why drinking makes you ravenous: alcohol switches on the brain's hunger neurons, makes food more rewarding, lowers blood sugar, and weakens self-control. Plus what actually helps.
metaDescription: Why does alcohol make you hungry? How it triggers hunger neurons, lowers blood sugar and fuels next-day cravings, plus simple ways to curb the munchies.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: why does alcohol make you hungry
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol makes you hungry because it switches on the same brain cells that normally fire when you're starving, it makes food smell and taste more rewarding, it can nudge your blood sugar down, and it loosens the self-control you'd normally use to say no to a 1 a.m. burrito. The next morning, poor sleep and a mild blood-sugar dip can keep the cravings going. None of this means something is wrong with you. It's a predictable, well-studied effect, and once you understand the pieces you can plan around it instead of fighting it.

**The quick version of what to do:** eat a real meal with protein and fat before you drink, have a planned snack ready instead of relying on whatever is open at midnight, alternate drinks with water, and eat a proper breakfast the next day rather than grazing on sugar. If you have diabetes or take blood-sugar medicine, alcohol-related low blood sugar is a genuine safety issue, so read the "when to see a doctor" section below.

> **This is general information, not medical advice.** **See a doctor if** you have diabetes or take insulin or sulfonylurea drugs and drink alcohol, you get shaky, sweaty, confused, or faint after drinking (signs of low blood sugar), you binge eat after drinking and feel out of control or distressed about it, or you notice constant extreme hunger, unexplained weight loss, or excessive thirst even when you haven't been drinking. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** someone who has been drinking is confused, very drowsy, unresponsive, having a seizure, or can't be woken up. Low blood sugar and alcohol poisoning can look alike and both need urgent care.

## Why Does Alcohol Make You Hungry? The Four Main Reasons

The "drunk munchies" are not one effect. They're several overlapping ones, and different people feel them to different degrees. Here's how they fit together.

1. **Alcohol activates the brain's hunger neurons.** A small group of cells in the hypothalamus, called AgRP neurons, act like a starvation alarm. Research in mice suggests alcohol can turn them on even when the body has plenty of fuel.
2. **Alcohol makes food more rewarding.** It heightens the brain's response to the smell and taste of food. This is called the aperitif effect, and it's the reason a pre-dinner drink was traditionally served to sharpen the appetite.
3. **Alcohol can lower your blood sugar.** While your liver is busy clearing alcohol, it's worse at releasing stored sugar into your blood. A dip in blood sugar is a strong hunger signal, especially if you didn't eat much.
4. **Alcohol lowers your inhibitions.** The part of your brain that weighs "do I really want this?" gets quieter after a few drinks, so cravings you'd normally ignore turn into a drive-through order.

The sections below take each one in turn, then look at the next-morning hunger that catches a lot of people off guard.

## Reason 1: Alcohol Flips On Your Brain's Starvation Signal (AgRP Neurons)

Deep in the brain, the hypothalamus acts as your body's fuel gauge. Inside it sit two groups of nerve cells that pull in opposite directions. One group (POMC neurons) helps you feel full. The other group, **AgRP neurons** (short for agouti-related peptide), drives hunger. When you haven't eaten for a while, AgRP neurons fire and create the urgent, hard-to-ignore pull toward food. In lab animals, switching these neurons on artificially makes even a well-fed mouse start eating right away.

The most cited study on alcohol and these cells came from researchers at the Francis Crick Institute in London, published in *Nature Communications* in 2017 (Cains and colleagues). They gave mice the equivalent of a weekend of drinking, and the mice ate noticeably more food. When the team looked at the brain, they found alcohol made AgRP neurons more active. They also showed that this activity was needed for the effect: when they blocked AgRP neuron activity, the alcohol-driven overeating largely went away.

What this means in plain terms: alcohol may be tricking a hard-wired hunger circuit into thinking you're low on fuel, even though alcohol itself carries a lot of calories (about 7 calories per gram, close to fat).

Two honest caveats belong here:

- **This was a mouse study.** Mouse and human hypothalamus work in similar ways, which is why the research is taken seriously, but it hasn't been shown in the same direct way in people. It's a strong explanation, not the final word.
- **It's not the only reason.** Even if AgRP neurons explain part of the effect, the reward, blood-sugar, and inhibition effects below add up on top of it.

## Reason 2: The Aperitif Effect Makes Food Smell and Taste Better

People have known for centuries that a drink before dinner makes you eat more. That's literally the job of an aperitif. Modern research backs it up.

Psychologists who study appetite, including Martin Yeomans's group at the University of Sussex, have run controlled studies where volunteers were given either an alcoholic drink or a non-alcoholic one before a meal. Across many of these experiments, people who had alcohol tended to eat more at the meal, and they usually didn't cut back later to make up for the extra calories from the drink.

A brain-imaging study from Indiana University, published in the journal *Obesity* in 2015 (Eiler and colleagues), gave women an intravenous infusion of alcohol or saline and then exposed them to food aromas while scanning their brains. With alcohol on board, brain areas involved in hunger and reward, including the hypothalamus, responded more strongly to food smells, and the women ate more at a meal afterward than they did after saline.

The practical takeaway: alcohol doesn't just make you hungrier, it makes food more appealing. That's why the smell of pizza at the end of a night out is so hard to walk past.

### Why the cravings lean toward salty, fatty, greasy food

Few people crave steamed broccoli after a night out. A few things push you toward heavy, salty food:

- **Reward chemistry.** Alcohol boosts dopamine and the brain's reward signaling. Energy-dense, salty, fatty food is the most rewarding food there is, so it stands out more.
- **Salt and fluid shifts.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you lose more fluid and some electrolytes. That may partly explain why salty food feels especially appealing, though this link is less well studied than the brain effects.
- **Availability and habit.** Late-night options tend to be fried, cheesy, and quick. A lot of what feels like a craving is just what's open.

## Reason 3: Alcohol Can Push Your Blood Sugar Down

This one is real chemistry, and it matters more than most articles admit.

Between meals, and especially overnight, your liver keeps your blood sugar steady by releasing stored glucose and by making new glucose from scratch (a process called gluconeogenesis). Alcohol interferes with that second job. When your liver breaks down alcohol, it uses up a helper molecule called NAD+. With less NAD+ available, the liver can't make new glucose as well.

For a healthy person who ate a decent meal, this usually causes only a mild dip, if any. But the dip is more likely when:

- you drank on an empty stomach or skipped dinner,
- you drank a lot over several hours,
- you exercised hard that day, which already drained your stored sugar,
- you're slim or haven't been eating much in general.

Lower blood sugar is one of the body's loudest hunger signals. It can show up as sudden, intense cravings for something sweet or starchy, sometimes with shakiness or irritability.

There's a second wrinkle with sugary drinks. Cocktails, sweet mixers, and alcopops can spike your blood sugar first, which triggers an insulin response, and then the alcohol makes it harder for your liver to top your blood sugar back up. Some people feel that as a crash and a wave of hunger an hour or two later.

**This is a safety issue for people with diabetes.** If you take insulin or certain diabetes pills (sulfonylureas such as glipizide or glyburide), alcohol can cause low blood sugar that is dangerous and can happen many hours after your last drink, including while you sleep. The symptoms of low blood sugar (confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness, clumsiness) look a lot like being drunk, so other people may not realize you need help. If this applies to you, talk to your doctor about a plan, and see our guide to [alcohol and blood sugar management](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

## Reason 4: Lower Inhibitions Turn Cravings Into Orders

Even if alcohol didn't change your hunger at all, it would still change your eating. The prefrontal cortex, the part of your brain behind planning and self-control, is one of the first areas alcohol dulls. That's the part that normally says "I'm not actually hungry, I'll eat tomorrow" or "I already had dinner."

With that voice turned down, a few things happen at once:

- **You act on small cravings** you'd normally ignore.
- **You stop tracking how much you've eaten.** Mindless snacking from a bowl at a party adds up quickly.
- **Social settings encourage it.** Late-night food is often part of the ritual, and it's easier to go along with the group.

This is why planning ahead works better than willpower. You're making the decision with a sober brain instead of leaving it to a tipsy one.

## Hormones: What Happens to Leptin and Ghrelin

You'll often read that alcohol "blocks leptin" (the fullness hormone) or "raises ghrelin" (the hunger hormone). The truth is messier.

- **Leptin.** Some small human studies have found leptin levels drop after drinking, which in theory would make you feel less full. Other studies haven't found a clear effect. It may play a supporting role, but it's not a settled explanation.
- **Ghrelin.** Studies on alcohol and ghrelin have given mixed results. Some have even found that alcohol lowers ghrelin in the short term, which is the opposite of what you'd expect if ghrelin were driving drunk hunger.
- **Sleep hormones.** The clearer link is indirect. Poor sleep is well known to shift appetite hormones in the direction of more hunger, and alcohol reliably makes sleep worse, which brings us to the next morning.

The honest summary: brain circuits, reward, blood sugar, and lowered inhibitions are better supported explanations than a simple "alcohol messes up your hunger hormones" story.

## Why Am I So Hungry the Day After Drinking?

Hangover hunger is its own thing, and many people find it stronger than the drunk munchies. Several causes overlap:

### Poor sleep drives appetite

Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it breaks up the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. Sleep research, including well-known studies by Spiegel and colleagues (2004) and Taheri and colleagues (2004), has linked short or poor sleep with lower leptin, higher ghrelin, and stronger appetite, especially for high-carb, high-calorie food. One rough night after drinking can tilt your appetite the same way. For more on why this happens, see our guide to [sleep for social drinkers](/never-hungover/sleep-optimization-social-drinkers-circadian-rhythm).

### Low blood sugar in the morning

The liver's reduced ability to make glucose can linger into the morning after a heavy night, especially if you didn't eat much. Waking up shaky and desperate for toast or pancakes is a common result.

### Dehydration can feel like hunger

Alcohol makes you lose fluid. Thirst and hunger signals overlap in the brain, and many people reach for food when what they really need is water and some electrolytes. Drinking a big glass of water first and waiting a few minutes can tell you which one you're feeling. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers when they help.

### Your body is recovering

Your body is doing repair work, from clearing alcohol by-products to calming low-grade inflammation. That work takes energy, and wanting a solid meal is a reasonable response.

### When you're NOT hungry the next day

The opposite is also common. Nausea, an irritated stomach lining, and a slower-emptying stomach can kill your appetite for hours. That's normal for a hangover. Try small, bland foods (toast, crackers, bananas, broth) and fluids, and build up from there. If you can't keep any fluids down for many hours, see the doctor section below.

## Does Alcohol Make You Gain Weight Because of the Hunger?

Partly, yes. The calories in the drinks are only half the story. The other half is the extra food.

- **Drinks are calorie-dense.** A standard drink has roughly 100 to 150 calories before you add mixers. Several drinks can equal a meal.
- **The extra food usually isn't offset.** Controlled studies on the aperitif effect have generally found that people eat more after alcohol and don't reliably eat less later to balance it out.
- **Your body burns alcohol first.** While your body is clearing alcohol, it burns less fat, so the fat from that late-night meal is more likely to be stored.
- **Next-day cravings stack on top.** A night of drinking can easily become a day and a half of eating more than you planned.

None of this means one night out ruins anything. It does explain why regular drinking makes weight management harder for a lot of people. Our guide to [alcohol and weight loss](/never-hungover/alcohol-weight-loss-metabolic-guide-2025) goes deeper on the metabolism side.

## How to Stop the Drunk Munchies: What Actually Works

You don't need perfect willpower. You need to set things up so the easy choice is a decent one.

### Before you drink

- **Eat a real meal.** Protein, fat, and fiber slow how fast alcohol reaches your blood and help keep blood sugar steady. Think chicken or fish with rice and vegetables, a bean chili, eggs and toast, or Greek yogurt with nuts. See our [what to eat before drinking guide](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) for specifics.
- **Don't "save calories" by skipping dinner.** It's the most common mistake. Drinking on an empty stomach makes the blood-sugar dip, the intoxication, and the later binge all worse.
- **Decide your late-night food in advance.** If you know you'll want something, pick it now: a sandwich in the fridge, a protein bar in your bag, leftovers ready to heat up.

### While you drink

- **Alternate each drink with water.** It slows your drinking, limits fluid loss, and gives you something to hold.
- **Pick lower-sugar drinks** if you notice a crash. Spirits with soda water or a dry wine tend to cause less of a spike than sugary cocktails.
- **Watch the bar snacks.** Salty snacks make you thirstier, which can lead to more drinking. If you snack, choose something with protein.
- **Set a drink limit before you start.** Fewer drinks means less of every effect on this page.

### After you get home

- **Eat your planned snack and drink water.** Something with protein and some carbs, like a turkey sandwich, eggs, or yogurt, will satisfy you better than chips.
- **Keep trigger foods out of easy reach.** If there's no ice cream in the freezer, you won't eat ice cream at 2 a.m.
- **Put the delivery app off your home screen** for the night if late-night ordering is your pattern.

### The next morning

- **Water first, then breakfast.** Rehydrate, then eat a real meal with protein and some slow carbs, such as eggs with whole-grain toast, oatmeal with nuts, or a breakfast burrito.
- **Avoid grazing on sugar.** Pastries and soda give a quick lift and then a slump, which brings the cravings back.
- **Get some daylight and an early night.** Better sleep the next night helps reset your appetite.

For the habits that do the most to reduce the morning after overall, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## When to See a Doctor

> **When to see a doctor:** Drunk hunger is normal, but some patterns deserve medical attention.
>
> - **You have diabetes** and drink, especially if you use insulin or sulfonylurea medicines. Ask your doctor how to drink more safely, how to check your blood sugar, and what to eat.
> - **You've had low blood sugar symptoms after drinking:** shaking, sweating, a racing heart, confusion, or fainting. This can happen even without diabetes after heavy drinking on an empty stomach.
> - **You binge eat after drinking and feel out of control,** ashamed, or distressed about it, or you eat large amounts often even without alcohol. A doctor or an eating-disorder specialist can help, and it's common to need support with this.
> - **You're extremely hungry or thirsty all the time,** urinating a lot, or losing weight without trying. These can be signs of diabetes or another condition and are worth checking regardless of drinking.
> - **You can't keep fluids down** for many hours the day after drinking, or you're vomiting blood or have severe stomach pain.
>
> **Get emergency help (911 in the US) if** someone is confused, very drowsy, hard to wake, breathing slowly, having a seizure, or unresponsive after drinking. Low blood sugar and alcohol poisoning can look similar and both need urgent treatment. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone.

## Can a Supplement Help With Drunk Hunger?

There's no good evidence that any supplement reliably stops the drunk munchies. Some appetite-related claims you'll see online are based on animal research or on nothing at all, so treat them with skepticism. The things that work are the boring ones above: a real meal beforehand, fewer drinks, water, a planned snack, and decent sleep.

Some people do use supplements to help with how they feel the next day. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, has been studied mostly in animals for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the brain, with limited human data. It's promising but not proven, and there's no good evidence that it reduces drunk hunger specifically. If you want to try DHM as part of your routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when. No supplement replaces eating before you drink or drinking less.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol makes you hungry through several effects at once: it activates hunger neurons in the brain (strongest evidence so far is in mice), makes food more rewarding, can lower your blood sugar, and weakens self-control.
- Next-day hunger comes mainly from poor sleep, a lingering blood-sugar dip, and dehydration that can feel like hunger.
- The best defense is planning: eat a proper meal first, alternate drinks with water, have a sensible snack ready, and eat a real breakfast.
- If you have diabetes, alcohol-related low blood sugar is a real danger that can strike hours later, so make a plan with your doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does alcohol make you hungry?**

Alcohol makes you hungry in several ways at once. Research in mice suggests it activates AgRP neurons, the brain cells that normally signal starvation. It also makes food smell and taste more rewarding (the aperitif effect), can lower your blood sugar by slowing the liver's glucose production, and dulls the self-control that normally stops you from acting on cravings.

**Why do I crave salty, greasy food when I'm drunk?**

Alcohol boosts the brain's reward response, and energy-dense salty, fatty food is the most rewarding food available, so it stands out more. Alcohol also makes you lose fluid and some electrolytes, which may make salty food feel extra appealing. And late-night options tend to be fried and cheesy, so availability plays a big part too.

**Why am I so hungry the day after drinking?**

Next-day hunger usually comes from poor sleep, which shifts appetite hormones toward more hunger, a lingering dip in blood sugar after the liver spent the night clearing alcohol, and dehydration, which can feel a lot like hunger. Drinking water first and then eating a real breakfast with protein usually helps more than grazing on sugary snacks.

**Does alcohol lower your blood sugar?**

It can. While your liver breaks down alcohol, it's less able to make new glucose, so blood sugar can drift down, especially if you drank on an empty stomach or drank heavily. For most healthy people this causes only a mild dip and some hunger. For people with diabetes who use insulin or sulfonylurea medicines, it can cause dangerous low blood sugar hours after drinking, so they should make a plan with their doctor.

**Is it bad to eat before bed after drinking?**

Not necessarily. A sensible snack with protein and some carbs, plus water, can help steady your blood sugar overnight. The problem is usually what and how much: a huge, greasy meal can upset your stomach and add a lot of calories. Planning a moderate snack in advance beats ordering whatever is open at 2 a.m.

**How do I stop eating so much when I drink?**

Eat a real meal with protein, fat, and fiber before you start, alternate each drink with water, set a drink limit in advance, and decide on your late-night snack before you go out. Keeping trigger foods out of easy reach at home and eating a proper breakfast the next day also help. Planning works better than relying on willpower after a few drinks.

**Why does alcohol make some people lose their appetite instead?**

Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and can slow stomach emptying, and a hangover often brings nausea. For some people that outweighs the hunger effects, especially the next morning. Small, bland foods and fluids are the usual way through it. If you can't keep fluids down for many hours or have severe stomach pain, see a doctor.

**Does DHM stop the drunk munchies?**

There's no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement reliably stops drunk hunger. DHM has been studied mostly in animals for its effects on alcohol metabolism, with limited human data. The approaches with real support are eating before you drink, drinking less, staying hydrated, and sleeping well.
